questions.stem: A 71 year old man has a CT of his kidneys for haematuria. The radiologist notes that the infrarenal aorta measures 3.4 cm in diameter, while the aorta just above the renal arteries measures 2.1 cm. The aortic wall is not separated into two lumens. He has no abdominal pain and his BP is 142/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A permanent dilation to at least 1.5 times the normal diameter (3.4 cm versus 2.1 cm) is an aneurysm; AAA is the commonest type and is usually infrarenal.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
3.4 divided by 2.1 is more than 1.5: that meets the definition.

elim: Would show an intimal flap with true and false lumens.
Dilation of less than 1.5 times normal diameter; this segment is over 1.5 times.
The infrarenal aorta is normally around 2 cm.
Gives a soft tissue cuff around the aorta that encases the ureters.

steps.x: Aneurysm = permanent dilation to at least 1.5 times normal diameter; AAA usually infrarenal.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man who smokes is found to have an asymptomatic expansile pulsatile mass on abdominal examination. His GP explains that this is the most common type of aortic aneurysm. Ultrasound is booked. His BP is 150/92 mmHg and pulse rate 76 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely location of the aneurysm?
questions.e: AAA is the most common type of aortic aneurysm and is typically infrarenal, presenting as a pulsatile abdominal mass.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely location of the aneurysm?

clues: expansile pulsatile mass on abdominal examination
most common type of aortic aneurysm
steps.x: Palpable in the abdomen and the most common type: below the renal arteries.

elim: Arch aneurysms are much less common and are not palpable in the abdomen.
Not palpable in the abdomen.
Suprarenal aneurysms are much less common than infrarenal ones.
Thoracoabdominal aneurysms are rare and extend above the diaphragm.

steps.x: AAA is the commonest aneurysm, typically infrarenal.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man asks his GP about his risk of an abdominal aortic aneurysm after a friend died from one. He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 40 years, has hypertension treated with amlodipine and a total cholesterol of 6.2 mmol/L. He has no family history of aneurysm and does not have diabetes.
questions.q: Which is the strongest risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm in this man?
questions.e: Smoking is the strongest risk factor for AAA; hypertension, atherosclerosis, chronic renal disease and family history also contribute.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the strongest risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm in this man?

clues: smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 40 years
steps.x: Several risk factors are present; the question asks for the strongest.

elim: Risk rises with age; younger age is not a risk factor.

A risk factor, but weaker than smoking.

steps.x: Strongest AAA risk factor: smoking.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man who has never smoked asks whether he should be checked for an abdominal aortic aneurysm. He has well-controlled asthma, gout and hypothyroidism. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. His father died aged 70 from a ruptured aortic aneurysm.
questions.q: Which feature of his history most increases his risk of abdominal aortic aneurysm?
o: Father died from a ruptured aneurysm
questions.e: Family history of AAA is a recognised risk factor, along with smoking, hypertension, atherosclerosis and chronic renal disease.

steps.x: The question asks: which feature of his history most increases his risk of abdominal aortic aneurysm?

clues: His father died aged 70 from a ruptured aortic aneurysm
steps.x: No smoking, so look for the other listed risk factors: family history.

elim: Not a risk factor for AAA.
Not a recognised risk factor for AAA.
Not a risk factor for AAA.

steps.x: AAA risk: smoking (strongest), hypertension, atherosclerosis, chronic renal disease, family history.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with long-standing hypertension has a 2 month history of difficulty swallowing solid food and a constant dull ache between his shoulder blades. He has not lost weight. He smokes. His chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum, and a CT shows a 6.5 cm dilated descending aorta compressing the oesophagus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A thoracic aortic aneurysm presents with chest or back pain and compression of surrounding structures, here the oesophagus causing dysphagia.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: 6.5 cm dilated descending aorta compressing the oesophagus
steps.x: Dull chest or back pain plus a compression symptom and a dilated aorta.

elim: Gives dysphagia for solids and liquids with a dilated oesophagus, not a dilated aorta.
Sudden tearing pain, not a 2 month dull ache.
Can compress the oesophagus, but the CT shows a dilated aorta.
Gives progressive dysphagia with weight loss and an oesophageal mass.

steps.x: Thoracic aortic aneurysm: chest pain and compression symptoms (dysphagia, hoarseness, cough).

questions.stem: A 67 year old man had a 4.6 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm found on screening. He is thin and has no symptoms. His BP is 138/82 mmHg and pulse rate 68 bpm regular. A medical student is asked to examine his abdomen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
o: Expansile pulsatile mass above the umbilicus
Tender mass in the right iliac fossa
questions.e: AAA classically presents as a pulsatile, expansile abdominal mass, best felt in thin patients above the umbilicus.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
The aorta bifurcates at the umbilicus, so the aneurysm is felt above it, expanding with each beat.

elim: Suggests gastric or pancreatic carcinoma.
Indicates ascites.
Suggests an appendix mass or caecal tumour.
Suggests bowel obstruction.

steps.x: AAA: pulsatile expansile abdominal mass on examination.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man collapsed briefly at home and now has severe left flank and back pain. He smokes and has had a stroke. His pulse rate is 122 bpm and BP 88/52 mmHg. He is pale, clammy and confused. A tender mass is felt in the upper abdomen. Investigations are shown below.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden collapse, flank and back pain, shock and a tender abdominal mass in an older male smoker is a ruptured AAA: a life-threatening emergency.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: severe left flank and back pain
steps.x: Older vascular man, flank/back pain and shock: ruptured AAA until proven otherwise.

elim: Gives left iliac fossa pain and fever, not collapse with a tender central mass.
Amylase is normal and the history is sudden collapse.
Does not cause shock and collapse in an older man; must not be assumed.
Recovers quickly and does not cause ongoing shock and flank pain.

steps.x: Ruptured AAA: sudden abdominal/back pain, hypotension, tachycardia; instability = emergency.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has a 6 hour history of severe back pain. He has bruising over his left flank and left groin. He has hypertension and smokes. His pulse rate is 116 bpm and BP 94/60 mmHg. There is a tender pulsatile mass in the epigastrium. His serum amylase is normal and urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Back pain, shock, flank and groin bruising from retroperitoneal blood and a tender pulsatile mass mean a ruptured AAA.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: bruising over his left flank and left groin
steps.x: The bruising tracks from retroperitoneal blood; with a pulsatile mass and shock, this is rupture.

elim: Can cause flank bruising but amylase is normal and the mass is pulsatile.
Does not cause shock, flank bruising or a pulsatile mass.
Fever and loin pain with a positive dipstick, without a pulsatile mass.
Gives progressive back pain, not shock and bruising.

steps.x: AAA rupture: abdominal/back pain, hypotension, tachycardia, pulsatile mass.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman who has smoked all her life has sudden severe central abdominal pain radiating to her back. She has never been screened. Her pulse rate is 130 bpm, BP 74/40 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. She is drowsy and mottled. Her abdomen is distended with a tender pulsatile mass.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: AAA is less common in women and they are not screened, but a lifelong smoker with back pain, shock and a pulsatile mass has a ruptured AAA.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
Female sex does not exclude AAA; screening is for men, so women present when it ruptures.

elim: Pain out of proportion with a soft abdomen, not a pulsatile mass.
Gives a rigid abdomen with free gas, not a pulsatile mass.
Occurs in women of reproductive age.
Gives distension and constipation with a coffee bean sign, not shock with a pulsatile mass.

steps.x: Rupture: sudden abdominal/back pain + shock; haemodynamic instability = life-threatening emergency.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man attends his NHS abdominal aortic aneurysm screening appointment. He has no symptoms. He is an ex-smoker with hypertension. The ultrasound shows an infrarenal aortic diameter of 3.8 cm. His BP is 144/86 mmHg.
questions.q: How is his scan result best classified?
questions.e: Under the NHS AAA screening programme, 3 to 4.4 cm is a small AAA, followed with a repeat ultrasound after 1 year.

steps.x: The question asks: how is his scan result best classified?
Use the bands: under 3 normal; 3–4.4 small; 4.5–5.4 medium; 5.5 or more large.

elim: Large means 5.5 cm or more.
Medium means 4.5 to 5.4 cm.
Normal means less than 3 cm.
He has no symptoms.

steps.x: Small AAA 3–4.4 cm: yearly ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man is having a routine abdominal examination at a hypertension clinic when the doctor feels a pulsatile mass above the umbilicus that expands with each heartbeat. He has no pain. He is an ex-smoker. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 152/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Abdominal ultrasound, measuring aortic diameter, is the first-line investigation for a suspected AAA.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
Stable, asymptomatic suspected AAA: measure it with ultrasound.

elim: May show wall calcification but cannot measure diameter accurately.
Assesses leg arterial disease.

Not a first-line test for AAA.

steps.x: AAA first-line: abdominal ultrasound measuring diameter.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man reads that his brother-in-law was found to have an aortic aneurysm. He asks his GP when he will be checked. He is an ex-smoker with no symptoms and a normal abdominal examination.
questions.q: When will he routinely be offered abdominal aortic aneurysm screening?
o: Only if he develops abdominal pain
Ultrasound in the year he turns 65
questions.e: The NHS AAA screening programme offers a one-off abdominal ultrasound to men in the year they turn 65; ultrasound is the gold standard for screening.

steps.x: The question asks: when will he routinely be offered abdominal aortic aneurysm screening?
National programme: men, ultrasound, the year they turn 65.

Not the national screening schedule.

steps.x: AAA screening: men in the year they turn 65, by ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man missed his abdominal aortic aneurysm screening invitation at 65 because he was working abroad. He has now returned and self-refers to the NHS screening programme. He is asymptomatic and smoked for 30 years.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Men over 65 who were not screened can self-refer; screening uses abdominal ultrasound, the gold standard for AAA screening.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate investigation?

clues: missed his abdominal aortic aneurysm screening
steps.x: Screening = ultrasound, whatever the age at which it is done.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with COPD has a 5.7 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound. He has been referred to the vascular team, who are deciding whether endovascular repair is possible. His FEV1 is 45% predicted. His eGFR is 72 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: CT angiography is the gold standard for surgical planning and determines anatomical suitability for EVAR (neck length, angulation, iliac access).

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate next investigation?
The decision is about anatomy for a stent graft; that needs CT angiography, and his kidneys allow contrast.

Assesses heart function but not EVAR anatomy.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with a known 5.2 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm has had 3 hours of moderate lower back pain. He is alert. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg, unchanged over an hour. His abdomen has a mildly tender pulsatile mass. His haemoglobin is 142 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: In a haemodynamically stable patient with a symptomatic AAA, an urgent CT angiogram looks for rupture and plans repair; unstable patients go straight to theatre.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate investigation?
Symptomatic but stable: there is time to image with CT before deciding on surgery.

elim: Assumes mechanical back pain in a man with a known aneurysm.
Slow and does not assess the aneurysm for leak.
Delays assessment of a symptomatic aneurysm.
Unsafe; symptomatic AAA must be imaged urgently.

steps.x: Stable symptomatic AAA: CT angiogram. Unstable: emergency surgery.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has an abdominal ultrasound as part of the NHS screening programme. He asks the sonographer what measurement is taken and what number would mean he has an aneurysm. He has no symptoms and is a non-smoker.
questions.q: Which ultrasound result would define an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
o: Maximum aortic diameter of 3 cm or more
Normal iliac artery diameter of 1 cm
questions.e: Ultrasound measures maximum aortic diameter; a diameter of 3 cm or more (about 1.5 times normal) defines an AAA.

steps.x: The question asks: which ultrasound result would define an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
AAA is defined by size: a diameter at least 1.5 times normal, 3 cm in the abdominal aorta.

A normal iliac size, not a definition of AAA.
Used for stenosis, not aneurysm.
Can occur in aneurysms but does not define one.

steps.x: AAA = aortic diameter 3 cm or more on ultrasound (at least 1.5 times normal).

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has his NHS abdominal aortic aneurysm screening ultrasound. The maximum aortic diameter is 2.4 cm. He is an ex-smoker with no symptoms. He asks when he will be scanned again.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Refer to vascular surgeons within 12 weeks
questions.e: A normal screening result (aorta under 3 cm) needs no further scanning or surgical consideration.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate management?
Under 3 cm is normal.

elim: For aneurysms of 3 cm or more.

For small AAA (3–4.4 cm).
For 5.5 cm or more, symptomatic or rapidly growing aneurysms.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has an incidental abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 3.9 cm on ultrasound. He has no symptoms. He has stopped smoking and his BP is 128/78 mmHg on ramipril. Previous scans are not available.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Vascular referral within 12 weeks and repeat ultrasound in 1 year
questions.e: Aneurysms over 3 cm are referred to vascular surgeons within 12 weeks; a small AAA (3–4.4 cm) has a repeat ultrasound after 1 year.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate management?
Small band, asymptomatic, no growth data.

For medium aneurysms of 4.5–5.4 cm.
For 5.5 cm or more, symptomatic or rapidly growing.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is under surveillance for an abdominal aortic aneurysm. It measured 4.9 cm a year ago and now measures 5.2 cm. He has no abdominal or back pain. He is fit and well, and his BP is 132/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Urgent referral for repair within 2 weeks
questions.e: A medium AAA (4.5–5.4 cm) that is asymptomatic and growing less than 1 cm per year is followed with ultrasound every 3 months.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate management?
Medium size, 0.3 cm growth in a year, no symptoms: surveillance.

elim: Aneurysms do not regress; follow-up continues.

Yearly scans are for small (3–4.4 cm) aneurysms.
For 5.5 cm or more, growth over 1 cm per year or symptoms.

steps.x: Medium AAA (4.5–5.4 cm): ultrasound every 3 months.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm. A year ago it measured 4.2 cm. Today's ultrasound shows 5.3 cm. He is otherwise well and has stopped smoking. His BP is 134/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: No change: repeat ultrasound in 1 year
Urgent referral for repair within 2 weeks
questions.e: Growth of more than 1 cm per year is an indication for urgent referral for surgery within 2 weeks, even though the diameter is below 5.5 cm.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate management?

clues: A year ago it measured 4.2 cm
steps.x: Size alone says surveillance, but growth of 1.1 cm in a year changes it.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has a 5.9 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm. CT angiogram shows anatomy suitable for either open or endovascular repair. He is a fit retired postman who walks 5 miles a day, with no heart or lung disease and no previous abdominal surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Open aortic repair is first-line for a fit patient with a large AAA; EVAR is reserved for those unsuitable for open repair.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate definitive management?
Large AAA, fit, normal abdomen: no reason to avoid open surgery.

elim: Surveillance is not appropriate at 5.9 cm.
An extra-anatomic bypass for occlusive disease, not aneurysm repair.

steps.x: Open repair first-line; EVAR if unsuitable for open repair.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has a 6.0 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. He has had three previous laparotomies for Crohn's disease and has an ileostomy. He is otherwise reasonably fit. CT angiogram shows anatomy suitable for a stent graft.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: EVAR is the alternative when open repair is unsuitable, including a hostile abdomen and stoma; it needs long-term imaging for endoleak.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate definitive management?
Hostile abdomen plus stoma: avoid a laparotomy.

elim: Usually first-line, but a hostile abdomen with a stoma makes open repair hazardous.
A 6.0 cm aneurysm needs repair.
For small aneurysms only.
Medical therapy alone does not prevent rupture.

steps.x: EVAR if open repair unsuitable: high anaesthetic risk, comorbidities, horseshoe kidney, stoma, hostile abdomen.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is brought in by ambulance with sudden abdominal and back pain. Bedside ultrasound shows a 7 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. His pulse rate is 126 bpm and BP 80/46 mmHg. Two large-bore cannulas are in place and the vascular surgeon and anaesthetist have been called.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate step?
o: Arrange CT angiogram before deciding on surgery
Crossmatch 6 units of blood and transfer to theatre
Give IV fluids to a systolic BP above 140 mmHg
Group and save only and admit to the ward
questions.e: A ruptured AAA requires crossmatching blood (commonly 6 units) and emergency surgery; an unstable patient goes to theatre without CT.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate immediate step?
Unstable rupture: prepare blood and operate.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has a 4.1 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm under yearly surveillance. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and his clinic BP is 162/96 mmHg. He asks what he can do himself to reduce the chance of the aneurysm needing surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?
o: Smoking cessation and blood pressure control
questions.e: Ongoing management of AAA includes smoking cessation and blood pressure control, which slow growth and reduce rupture risk.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate additional management?
He has two modifiable factors that drive aneurysm growth.

Not indicated for a 4.1 cm aneurysm.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has open repair of a 6.2 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. Histology of the excised wall shows thinning of the media with fragmentation and loss of elastic fibres and collagen, and an infiltrate of macrophages and lymphocytes. There is no evidence of infection.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the aneurysm?
o: Bacterial infection of the aortic wall
Enzymatic degradation of elastin and collagen by matrix metalloproteinases
Intimal tear with a false lumen
Medial necrosis from a fibrillin defect
Syphilitic endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
questions.e: AAA results from degradation of elastin and collagen in the media, driven by matrix metalloproteinases and chronic inflammation, weakening the wall so it progressively dilates.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism of the aneurysm?

clues: loss of elastic fibres and collagen
steps.x: Loss of the wall's structural proteins plus inflammatory cells: enzymatic breakdown of the media.

elim: A mycotic aneurysm would show organisms or abscess; there is no infection.

steps.x: AAA pathophysiology: MMP and inflammation degrade elastin and collagen, weakening the wall.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with a 4.3 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm has poorly controlled hypertension. His aneurysm grew faster than expected last year. His GP explains that lowering his blood pressure should help slow the growth.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which hypertension accelerates aneurysm growth?
o: Increased wall stress on the weakened aortic wall
Reduced elastin synthesis by the liver
questions.e: Hypertension and atherosclerosis accelerate aneurysm growth by increasing wall stress on a wall already weakened by elastin and collagen loss.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism by which hypertension accelerates aneurysm growth?
Higher pressure pushes harder on an already weak wall.

elim: Hypertension does not raise viscosity.
Does not act on the aortic wall.
Hypertension does not reduce output or cause dilation.
Elastin is made locally in the vessel wall, not by the liver.

steps.x: Hypertension and atherosclerosis accelerate AAA growth via increased wall stress.

questions.stem: Two men have asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysms and the same BP of 140/85 mmHg. One aneurysm measures 4.0 cm and the other 6.5 cm. A student asks why the rupture risk of the larger one is many times higher, not just a little higher.
questions.q: Which principle best explains this?
o: Bernoulli's principle that pressure falls as velocity rises
Poiseuille's law that flow depends on the fourth power of radius
Wall tension is proportional to pressure multiplied by radius
questions.e: Laplace's law: for the same pressure a larger aneurysm has higher wall tension, so rupture risk rises disproportionately with diameter, which is why repair is offered at 5.5 cm.

steps.x: The question asks: which principle best explains this?
Same pressure, bigger radius: more tension on the wall.

elim: Explains flow through stenoses, not wall tension.
Describes gas diffusion across membranes.
Describes the relation between preload and stroke volume.
Describes resistance to flow in a tube, not wall tension.

steps.x: Laplace's law: tension ∝ pressure × radius; rupture risk climbs steeply with diameter.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man with ischaemic heart disease and an ejection fraction of 30% has a 6.1 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. The vascular team recommends endovascular repair through the femoral arteries rather than open repair. His son asks why this is safer in the short term.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason?
o: It avoids a major laparotomy and aortic cross-clamping
It completely removes the aneurysm sac
It uses no contrast or radiation
questions.e: EVAR reduces perioperative mortality compared with open repair by avoiding a major laparotomy, but carries a higher long-term risk of re-intervention for endoleak.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely reason?
Short-term safety comes from avoiding the big operation; the trade-off is long-term endoleak.

elim: The sac is left in place and excluded.
EVAR needs long-term imaging because of endoleak risk.
EVAR has a higher long-term re-intervention rate than open repair.
EVAR uses contrast and X-ray guidance.

steps.x: EVAR: lower perioperative mortality (no laparotomy), more re-intervention (endoleak).
